name: Swiss Design
basis: why/how: the picture is 'a plain line screen of black bars' whose height is local darkness
note: Grid, red shape and type are the style; only the line-screen photograph is a process. A line screen is a one-dimensional halftone.

lumenary.blurb: International style: a strict grid, a line-screen photograph, one red shape and bold sans type.

facts.bestOn: Strong, simple compositions with a clear tonal range

why: Swiss designers believed that a clear grid and honest photography could communicate more than decoration. So the page here is built on a six column grid, the picture is rendered as a plain line screen of black bars, and a single red shape and heavy sans-serif title do all the rest. Everything lines up, and nothing is there by accident.
how: Set a six column grid and place the picture across columns two to six.
Draw the picture as horizontal rows of thin vertical bars, whose height is the local darkness.
Let bright areas have no bars and dark areas fill the row.
Place one red shape across the picture’s edge.
Set the title flush left at the size that spans the picture, with small text, a rule and a page number on the same grid.
history: The International Typographic Style grew in Switzerland in the 1940s and 50s through designers such as Josef Müller-Brockmann, Armin Hofmann and Emil Ruder. The typeface Helvetica appeared in 1957, and the journal Neue Grafik spread the ideas worldwide. Its principles, grid, sans-serif type and objective photography, still underpin much of modern graphic design.
terms: An invisible set of columns and rows that every element is aligned to.
Text lined up on its left edge, with a ragged right edge.
A way of printing tone as lines whose thickness changes.
paragraphs: Swiss design is built on a grid, and this treatment puts the photograph on one. The page has a six-column grid; the picture takes columns two to six in the upper part. It is drawn as a line screen: a set of horizontal lines, each one a row of thin vertical bars whose height is the local darkness. Bright areas have no bars and dark areas fill the row, so the picture is made only of straight black marks.

One red shape straddles the edge of the picture. The title is set in a heavy sans-serif, flush left on the margin, at the size that makes it span the picture’s width; small lines of set text, a rule and a page number are placed on the same grid.

equations.note: Height of the bar at column x on line i; the lines are Δy apart.
Title size: c is the column width and w₁₀₀ the title’s measured width at size 100.

presets.text: A red square instead of a circle changes the whole balance.
Fewer lines make a coarser, more graphic picture.
Turn on the black ground for a night edition.
